stops.name: Cajamarca, the rooms filled twice with silver
stops.campa: The silver follows, twice the promised measure, hauled down from Cusco and the mining camps of the sierra on the backs of thousands of llamas driven by subjects who still, in these weeks, obey their captive Inca's word before any Spaniard's. Between gold and silver the company divides some twenty-four tons of treasure: an empire's temple-wealth converted, plank and idol and drinking-vessel alike, into the coin and plate of Castile. Atahualpa has kept his word to the letter. It buys him not one further day of the freedom he bargained for.

stops.name: Cajamarca, the trial and the garrote of the Inca
stops.campa: Charged before a hastily convened court with idolatry, the murder of his brother Huáscar, and plotting an army against his captors, the last charge got up out of rumor and fear, Atahualpa is condemned to burn. Friar Valverde offers him baptism to buy a mercy: the rope instead of the flame. He accepts, takes the name Francisco after his captor, and is garroted the same night in the plaza where he was seized eight months before. Pizarro, some chroniclers record, mourns him after the fact and wears black; the mourning changes nothing that the gold has already bought.

stops.name: Jauja, the first camp of the march
stops.campa: The column marches up out of Cajamarca along the Inca royal road, through passes and rope bridges built for llama trains, not horses, and makes its first extended camp in the fertile valley of Jauja, high, cold, and rich with maize terraces. Pizarro leaves a garrison and the sick here under Riquelme with the still-unassayed remainder of the treasure, and considers, briefly, founding his capital on this very plain before the lowland coast is even known to him. Ahead lies Cusco, and General Quisquis's army, still loyal to the dead Atahualpa's cause, falling back before them into the sierra.

stops.name: Cusco, entry into the navel of the world
stops.campa: Pizarro rides into Huacaypata, the great plaza of Cusco, Qosqo, the navel of the world, at the head of a column too small, by any ordinary reckoning, to have taken an empire ten thousand miles long. The city falls without a battle: General Quisquis has already withdrawn north, and the survivor prince Manco Inca, spared his brother's massacre, rides in at Pizarro's side, ready to be crowned as the puppet who will keep the provinces quiet a little longer. The stones of the Coricancha, still sheathed in gold, wait a day's grace before the stripping begins.

stops.name: Cusco, the Coricancha stripped, Manco Inca crowned
stops.campa: The Coricancha, temple of the Sun, is stripped of its golden sheeting, its garden of golden maize, the mummies of dead emperors robbed of the ornament they were dressed in for their long death-in-life. Days later, on the sixteenth of December, Pizarro sets the fringe of royal office on Manco Inca's brow in the plaza below and names him Sapa Inca under the Emperor Charles: a coronation staged to hold the empire's obedience through a Spanish mouth. Manco will wear the crown ten years, three in outward peace, before the rope of that same borrowed sovereignty snaps.

stops.name: Lima, Ciudad de los Reyes founded
stops.campa: Cusco, high and landlocked, cannot serve a governor who must answer to Seville by ship. Pizarro rejects Jauja too and rides down to the green valley of the Rímac, near the sea and its own good river, and on the eighteenth of January, near the feast of the Three Kings, traces with his own hand the grid of streets and the plaza mayor of a new capital, named Ciudad de los Reyes, the City of Kings, though history will keep the older Quechua name, Lima, for the river that waters it. It will outlive every other stone he lays.

stops.name: Cusco, Almagro returns from Chile, the city seized
stops.campa: Almagro, the ransomed partner of the pact of three, comes back exhausted and empty-handed from a ruinous expedition into the deserts of Chile to find that Cusco, which he believes his own by the letter of a rival grant from the Crown, has been claimed instead for the Pizarros. He raises the men of his broken expedition, marches on the city while Hernando and Gonzalo Pizarro hold it for their brother, and takes it by force, imprisoning both. Two Extremaduran captains of the same conquering enterprise now hold the same capital at each other's throats.

stops.name: Las Salinas, the battle for Cusco
stops.campa: On the white salt flats southeast of Cusco, Hernando and Gonzalo Pizarro's army meets Almagro's in the open, cavalry charging across ground bare and firm in the April dry season. Rodrigo Orgóñez, Almagro's field commander, is killed in the first hour; Almagro himself, too weak with illness to fight from the saddle, is taken from his litter. Francisco Pizarro, who has stayed at Lima through the whole civil quarrel, receives the news of the victory his brothers have won for him over the ransomed partner who once staked his own fortune to send four brothers across an ocean.

stops.name: Cusco, the garrote of Almagro
stops.campa: Old and broken in his cell, Almagro is tried, condemned, and garroted on Hernando Pizarro's order. Francisco does not countermand it, and history will not let him disclaim it. Almagro is then beheaded, his head set up in the plaza he once seized by force, a warning to any partner who mistakes friendship for a fixed share of an empire. The pact of three signed in a Panamá church fourteen years before ends here, one signer dead by the rope, another soon to answer for it with his own blood, the third, Luque, already some years in his grave.

stops.name: Lima, the palace, the cross of blood
stops.campa: Twenty armed Almagristas, avenging the father's garrote on the son's behalf, storm Pizarro's palace on the plaza after Sunday dinner. Most of his guests flee down the stairs; his half-brother Martín de Alcántara and a handful of servants fight and die at the door while the old governor, past sixty, struggles to buckle on his breastplate too late. He kills two attackers and runs a third through before exhaustion and a sword-thrust to the throat bring him down. Falling, he draws a cross on the floor in his own blood, kisses it, and dies crying the one word: Jesús.
stops.quote_source: Agustín de Zárate, Historia del descubrimiento y conquista del Perú (1555), on Pizarro's last cry

stops.name: Lima, burial amid the city he founded
stops.campa: The city he traced six years before with his own hand buries him in haste and fear, the Almagrista faction now ruling the plaza he founded, his loyal friends scattered or in hiding. He is laid, the tradition says, wrapped in a cloak and interred without ceremony in the cathedral he had begun to raise on the same square: the marqués of an empire, murdered in his own hall by the sons of the partner his brothers had garroted, given the burial of a man nobody now dares to mourn aloud.

stops.name: Lima Cathedral, the skull in the crypt, the false glass coffin
stops.campa: For eighty-six years, since 1891, a body identified as Pizarro's has lain on public view in a glass-sided coffin in the cathedral, embalmed and displayed for the pious and the curious alike. In 1977, workmen cleaning a forgotten crypt beneath the cathedral floor uncover a lead box inscribed: here is the skull of the Marquis Don Francisco Pizarro, who discovered and won Peru, and placed it under the crown of Castile, alongside a second box holding a jumble of other bones, dismembered like a relic long fought over. The glass coffin's occupant, it now seems certain, is someone else entirely.
